chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Yazid ibn Ishaq from Harun ibn Hamzah said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who hired a laborer, and one of them did not trust the other, so he placed the wage in the hand of a third party; that man died and left no guarantor, and the wage was consumed. He said: 'The employer is liable for the laborer's wage until he pays it, unless the laborer called him to that and accepted the man; if he did, then his right is where he placed it and accepted it.'
From him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Abu Abdillah al-Jamurani from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abdullah ibn Waddah said:

There was a transaction between me and a Jew, and he cheated me by a thousand dirhams. I brought him before the governor and made him swear, and he swore, though I knew he swore an oath of perjury. After that, profits and many dirhams of his remained with me. I wanted to take the thousand dirhams that were mine from him and swear an oath regarding them. I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) informing him that I had made him swear and he had sworn, and property of his was with me, and if he ordered me to take the thousand dirhams he swore upon, I would do so. He wrote back (peace be upon him): 'Do not take anything from him. If he wronged you, do not wrong him. If it were not that you accepted his oath and made him swear, I would have ordered you to take from under your hand. But since you accepted his oath, the oath has gone with what is in it.' So I did not take anything from him and I adhered to the letter of Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him).
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on an employer's liability for wages if the worker dies, and how does accepting a debtor's oath affect property seizure?
ai.summary: In the first narration, Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that the employer bears the risk of the guarantor's insolvency unless the worker explicitly consents to the substitution, reflecting the Shia principle of preserving the creditor's right to choose their security. The second narration, transmitted via the Imam's written reply, establishes that accepting an oath in court constitutes a final settlement of the debt, preventing the creditor from later seizing assets for that specific claim, even if the oath was perjurious, thereby emphasizing the legal finality of the sworn statement.
